title: Raga Bhairao
hookLine: a serious morning raga that opens with one plain line: nothing happens outside you

cards: The alarm goes off, and before your feet find the floor the day already has weight. A hard conversation at ten. A hospital visit after lunch.

A letter that can't wait another week. Not every morning is bright and bouncy, and pretending otherwise doesn't help. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga for mornings like that: Bhairao, sometimes written Bhairo.
Tradition gives it a grave, unhurried mood, sung early, when the day is still deciding what it will be.

teach.h: AFTER KEDARA: EVENING TURNS TO MORNING.
teach.b: In the Granth's order, Bhairao comes right after Kedara, yesterday's dusk raga, so the book turns a page from evening to morning.

teach.h: GURUS AND BHAGATS IN ONE SECTION.
teach.b: Its pages hold hymns by Gurus and by Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, Kabir and Namdev among them; one of those is for tomorrow. Today, the door in.
The section begins with a hymn of Guru Nanak, and its first line is almost too plain to notice.
In paraphrase: nothing happens outside of you. You make it, you watch over it, and you know it. No storm, no miracle.
Just a sentence about who holds the day. Now hear it with a serious morning in mind. The hard conversation is still at ten.
The line doesn't cancel it. It changes the size of the room it happens in. The conversation, the hospital, the letter, all of it sits inside something larger, made and watched and known.

teach.h: SERIOUS CAN MEAN HONEST, NOT GLOOMY.
teach.b: Serious doesn't have to mean gloomy.
A serious morning can be an honest one: you see the weight clearly, and you also see you're not the only one holding it. That may be why tradition hears gravity in Bhairao rather than sadness.

Teachers describe the moods of ragas in different ways, so hold the mood as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. What is written is the line: nothing outside you. That's today's line: serious morning.

how: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Bhairao section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Bhairao, and tradition associates the raga with the early part of the day.

o: a raga sung early, with a grave and steady mood
a joyful raga sung to greet a wedding party
a lullaby raga sung as children fall asleep

games.q: what's inside the raga — tap the pairs.

s: a serious raga has to be a sad one
tradition hears gravity in Bhairao, not gloom: serious can mean honest.
in the Granth's order, Bhairao follows Kedara
the book turns from yesterday's dusk raga to a morning one.
Bhairao holds only hymns by the Gurus
it also holds Bhagat hymns, Kabir's and Namdev's among them.

games.q: a hard day is coming and you can't move it. what does Bhairao's opening line offer?
o: a promise that the hard thing will be cancelled.
a reminder that nothing happens outside the One.
advice to stay in bed until it passes.
games.why: Guru Nanak's line doesn't remove the weight. it says the whole day, weight and all, is made, watched and known.

practice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Bhairao, or simply sit in the quiet, and silently name the heaviest thing waiting for you today.
Don't solve it; lay it in front of you like a letter face up on a table, and let the breath go long and slow around it.
If you pray, hold Guru Nanak's opening thought beside it, that nothing happens outside the One; if you don't, simply notice that the thing is there and you are still breathing.

wordCard.voice: Raga Bhairao. The section that follows Kedara in the Granth, a raga tradition sings early with a grave, steady mood, opening with Guru Nanak's line that nothing happens outside the One. Today's word.

orig.note: bhairao, the raga that follows Kedara in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: serious morning. A heavy day can be serious without being the whole sky. More tomorrow.
